system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2125-09-10 01:56:00 to 2125-09-12 17:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, and chronic back pain was admitted with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and hyperglycemia leading to diabetic ketoacidosis. The episode was likely triggered by recent emotional stress after disclosing childhood sexual abuse. She was managed in the ICU with IV fluids and insulin, then transitioned to the medicine floor. Her insulin regimen was adjusted due to hypoglycemia, reducing Lantus from 24 to 17 units nightly. Gabapentin was restarted for chronic pain at a low dose to avoid exacerbating gastroparesis. Nausea improved with supportive care and resumption of metoclopramide. A urine culture showed coagulase-negative staph without signs of infection, so no antibiotics were given. She stabilized, tolerated a full diet, and was discharged home with follow-up plans for diabetes management, mental health support, and medication adjustments.
problems: Diabetes with ketoacidosis, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Diabetes with other specified manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Diabetes with renal manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looked like coffee grounds. I’ve been vomiting all day. I woke up with high blood sugar and just couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, right? That can definitely make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I’ve had this before. But the coffee ground part scared me. Is there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about that. Your CT scan showed some changes in the esophagus, possibly from vomiting. We’ll need an endoscopy to check for any tears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An endoscopy? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s important to rule out serious bleeding. We also started you on a medication to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. My stomach pain is gone now, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We also placed a line in your groin because we couldn’t get an IV in your arm. It’s temporary and will help us give you fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that. It’s a bit uncomfortable, but I understand why it’s needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. Your labs show your blood sugar was high earlier, but it’s coming down. We’re giving you insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take Lantus at night. Should I still take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you’re not eating, we held your Lantus last night. We’ll restart it gradually. You’re getting Humalog for now based on your sugar levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I just don’t want my sugar to crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. No signs of low sugar so far. We also saw your potassium was low, so we’re giving supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is phosphorus low too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both were low. We’re replacing them through your IV. It should correct over the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been anxious—my heart’s been racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your heart rate was high earlier, in the 140s. But when you rested, it came down. It seems related to anxiety, not a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That happens when I’m stressed. Being in the ICU is overwhelming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll move you to the regular floor soon. It’s quieter and should help you relax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just had your endoscopy. The good news is no active bleeding. There’s a small erosion at the junction of your esophagus and stomach, likely from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the coffee grounds were from that? Not a serious bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s called a Mallory-Weiss tear—small and usually heals on its own. We’ll keep you on a strong acid blocker to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start eating soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance slowly. Your gastroparesis means your stomach empties slowly, so we have to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll be patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Potassium and phosphorus are normal now. Blood sugar is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’ve been sipping broth and haven’t vomited since yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll try a soft diet today. We also restarted your metoclopramide to help your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. It helps, but sometimes makes me restless.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch for that. If it happens, we can adjust. Your insulin dose is back to normal—20 units Lantus tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about my diabetes being off track again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need you to monitor sugars closely at home. Same with potassium—your levels dropped this time, so your doctor may check it in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting for a few days because of the femoral line site. Otherwise, resume normal activities as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We removed the femoral line this morning—no issues. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What meds should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your usual insulin—Lantus 20 units at night, Humalog with meals. Take metoclopramide with meals, gabapentin twice daily, and Zofran if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lisinopril for blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that daily. Follow up with your primary doctor in a week for labs and to review everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. If you vomit again or see dark stools, come back right away. Otherwise, take care and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here if you need us. You’re discharged now—someone will help you with the paperwork.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, and anxiety was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and one episode of coffee ground emesis. She was initially managed in the ICU with IV access via femoral line due to difficulty with peripheral access. A CT scan showed esophageal wall thickening and pneumobilia, but no acute abdominal process. An upper endoscopy revealed no active bleeding, with erosions at the gastroesophageal junction attributed to retching. The coffee ground emesis was determined to be from a small Mallory-Weiss tear. Her insulin regimen was adjusted during fasting, with Lantus held initially and later resumed at her home dose of 20 units. Electrolyte imbalances, including hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia, were corrected. Anxiety-related tachycardia improved with reassurance and transfer to the medicine floor. She tolerated oral intake, was weaned off IV support, and discharged home on her baseline medications with follow-up plans for glucose and electrolyte monitoring.
